Circuit of Fig-11(a) is the elementary complementary MOS (CMOS) inverter.

1. Transistor assignment  
   • M2 : p–channel MOSFET (pMOS). Source is tied to the positive rail VDD, drain is the common output node Vout, gate is driven by Vin.  
   • M1 : n–channel MOSFET (nMOS). Source is tied to ground, drain is tied to Vout, gate is driven by the same Vin.

   The two drains are shorted, therefore Vout is either connected to VDD through M2 or to GND through M1.

2. Logic (dc) behaviour  

   Vin = 0 (logic “0”)  
   – M1 : VGS = 0  ⇒  OFF  
   – M2 : VSG = VDD  (> |VTP|)  ⇒  ON  
   → Vout is pulled up to VDD (logic “1”).  

   Vin = VDD (logic “1”)  
   – M1 : VGS = VDD  (> VTN)  ⇒  ON  
   – M2 : VSG = 0    ⇒  OFF  
   → Vout is pulled down to 0 V (logic “0”).  

   Thus the circuit inverts the input: (0 → 1, 1 → 0).

3. Static power dissipation  
   In either dc state exactly one device is OFF, so there is no direct current path from VDD to ground.  
   Pstatic ≈ Ileak · VDD ≈ few nW; practically zero for ideal devices.

4. Transition (Vin between 0 and VDD)  

   When Vin is between VTN and VDD – |VTP| both transistors conduct simultaneously.  
   The dc transfer characteristic is obtained by equating the drain currents

          IDn = IDp

      βn (Vin – VTN)²            (NMOS saturated)
      ----------------  =  βp (VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²      (pMOS saturated)
               2

      with  βn = μn Cox (W/L)n,  βp = μp Cox (W/L)p.

   Solving for the switching (mid-point) voltage VM gives

          √βn (VM – VTN) = √βp (VDD – VM – |VTP|)

          VM = [ √βp (VDD – |VTP|) + √βn VTN ] / (√βn + √βp)

   • If |VTP| ≈ VTN and W/L is chosen so that βp ≈ βn  
     (remember μn ≈ 2-3 μp, so the p-device has to be 2-3× wider),  
     VM ≈ VDD / 2 – a very desirable symmetric switching point.

5. Noise margins (for a symmetric design)  

      VOH ≈ VDD , VOL ≈ 0  
      VIH , VIL obtained at |dVout/dVin| = 1 → both ≈ VM ≈ VDD/2.  

      NMH = VOH – VIH ≈ VDD/2  
      NML = VIL – VOL ≈ VDD/2

   Large (≈ half-rail) noise margins are one of the great advantages of the CMOS inverter.

6. Dynamic aspects  

   Only during switching is there simultaneous current through M2 and M1.  
   The average dynamic power for a capacitive load CL, switching with probability α at frequency f, is

          Pdyn = α CL VDD² f .

7. Summary of the analysis  

   • Function: logical NOT (inverter).  
   • Rail-to-rail output levels: VOH = VDD, VOL = 0.  
   • Zero static power in the two logic states.  
   • High noise immunity; VM can be centred at VDD/2 by sizing M2 ≈ 2-3 × M1.  
   • Very large input impedance, so it can easily drive many similar gates.

This makes the complementary (CMOS) inverter the fundamental building block of practically all modern digital integrated circuits.

Let  

• M2 = n-channel MOSFET (NMOS)  
• M1 = p-channel MOSFET (PMOS)  

The two devices are in series between VDD and ground and their gates are shorted to the input Vin.  
Vout is the common node between them.

1. Vin = 0 V (logic “0”)  

   NMOS M2  
   VGS2 = Vin – VDD = –VDD < VTN  ⇒  M2 is OFF.  

   PMOS M1  
   VGS1 = Vin – Vout = –Vout.  
   The device is ON only while |VGS1| = Vout > |VTP|.  
   If Vout happened to be high from a previous state, M1 will conduct and pull Vout down until  
        Vout ≈ |VTP| (≈ 0.5–0.7 V)  
   At that point |VGS1| = |VTP| and the PMOS turns OFF.  

   Result: no path to ground after Vout has fallen to |VTP|, and no path at all to VDD.  
   The “low” output therefore settles at about one threshold-voltage above ground, not at 0 V.

2. Vin = VDD (logic “1”)  

   NMOS M2  
   VGS2 = Vin – VDD = 0 < VTN  ⇒  M2 is OFF.  

   PMOS M1  
   VGS1 = VDD – Vout  (a positive value)  
   VGS1 is greater than VTP (which is negative), so the inequality VGS1 < VTP is not satisfied;  
   therefore the PMOS is also OFF.  

   Result: both transistors are OFF, Vout is completely floating and can be anywhere between
   0 V and VDD depending on stray charge—there is no defined logic “1”.

3. Intermediate Vin  

   Because the upper device is an NMOS whose source sits at VDD, its VGS is always
   Vin – VDD, which is ≤ 0 for every possible Vin, so the NMOS is never ON.
   Consequently there is never a conductive path from VDD to the output node.  
   The only current path that can exist is the PMOS discharging Vout toward ground, and even that path turns itself off when Vout reaches |VTP|.

Summary of the steady-state behaviour  

• Vin = 0 V  →  Vout ≈ |VTP| (not a valid 0)  
• Vin = VDD  →  Vout floating (undefined, not a valid 1)  

Therefore the network of Fig. 11(a) does NOT function as a CMOS inverter.  
To obtain a proper inverter one must place the PMOS at the top (to act as a pull-up) and the NMOS at the bottom (to act as a pull-down), which is exactly the arrangement shown in Fig. 11(b).

Figure 11(a) is nothing more than the basic CMOS inverter:

•  M2 is a p–channel MOSFET (pull-up, source at VDD).  
•  M1 is an n–channel MOSFET (pull-down, source at ground).  
•  The two gates are tied to the input Vin, and their drains are tied together to form the output node Vout.

1. Static operating points  

   a) Vin ≈ 0  
      – VGSN = 0 < VTN  →  M1 OFF  
      – VSGP = VDD > |VTP| →  M2 ON (linear)  
      → Vout is charged to VDD (logic “1”).  
      No dc current flows once the node is charged.

   b) Vin ≈ VDD  
      – VSGP = 0 < |VTP| →  M2 OFF  
      – VGSN = VDD > VTN  →  M1 ON (linear)  
      → Vout is discharged to 0 V (logic “0”).  
      Again, no static current flows after the transition.

2. Transition region (Vin between the two rails)  

   Both devices conduct momentarily, creating a current path from VDD to ground.  
   Writing the saturation-mode drain currents

        IDN = (βn/2)(Vin – VTN)²
        IDP = (βp/2)(VDD – Vin – |VTP|)²

   and equating IDN = IDP gives the switching (mid-point) voltage

        VM = [√βp (VDD – |VTP|) + √βn VTN] / (√βn + √βp)

   With βn ≈ 2–3 βp (to compensate for lower hole mobility) the designer can make VM ≈ VDD/2, giving nearly equal noise margins.

3. Static transfer characteristic  

   VOH ≈ VDD, VOL ≈ 0  
   VIL and VIH are obtained from |dVout/dVin| = 1.  
   Because the transition is steep, the noise margins  

        NMH = VOH – VIH      NML = VIL – VOL  

   are large (often > 0.45 VDD for well-sized devices).

4. Dynamic behaviour  

   • Propagation delay is set by charging/discharging the load capacitance CL through the
     on-resistances of M2 (tPLH) and M1 (tPHL).  Roughly,

        tPLH ≈ (CL VDD) / (βp (VDD – |VTP|)²)
        tPHL ≈ (CL VDD) / (βn (VDD – VTN)²)

   • Dynamic power: Pdyn = CL VDD² fSW.  
   • Short-circuit power (while both devices conduct) is usually a small fraction of Pdyn and is
     proportional to βn, βp and the input-transition time.

5. Key points of the analysis  

   • Rail-to-rail output swing.  
   • Essentially zero static power dissipation.  
   • High noise immunity.  
   • Delay and power scale mainly with capacitive loading and supply voltage.  

This behaviour explains why the complementary inverter of Fig. 11(a) is the fundamental building block of all static CMOS logic families.

Figure 11(a) is a proper CMOS inverter:  
• PMOS (upper device) has its source tied to the highest potential (VDD) so that its P-body/source junction is always reverse-biased.  
• NMOS (lower device) has its source tied to the lowest potential (GND) so that its N-body/source junction is reverse-biased.  
Whichever transistor is ON makes a low-resistance path between Vout and the corresponding supply rail while the other device is OFF, producing the familiar rail-to-rail transfer curve.

In Figure 11(b) the two transistors are still driven by the same input, but they have been connected “upside-down”:

 M1 (the upper transistor) is an NMOS whose ​source​ is connected to VDD.  
 M2 (the lower transistor) is a PMOS whose ​source​ is connected to GND.

Let Vin vary only between the legal logic levels 0 V and VDD (the normal operating range in a digital system).

1. Behaviour of the upper NMOS, M1  
   Source voltage VS = VDD  
   Gate voltage VG = Vin  
   VGS = VG – VS = Vin – VDD ≤ 0 for any Vin ≤ VDD  
   Because VGS can never exceed the NMOS threshold Vtn (≈0.6–0.8 V), M1 is **always OFF** in the normal input range.

2. Behaviour of the lower PMOS, M2  
   Source voltage VS = 0 V  
   Gate voltage VG = Vin  
   VSG = VS – VG = –Vin ≤ 0 for any Vin ≥ 0  
   VSG never reaches the magnitude of the PMOS threshold |Vtp|, so M2 is **always OFF** in the normal input range.

3. Consequence for the output node  
With both transistors cut off, there is no dc path from Vout to either rail.  
 • Vout is left floating (high-impedance).  
 • The gate cannot generate a valid logic-high or logic-low level by itself.  
 • Whatever logic level was stored on any load capacitance will simply stay there until it leaks away or is disturbed by the next stage.

4. What happens outside the 0–VDD range?  
If Vin were (improperly) driven beyond the rails, one or the other device could turn on:  
 • Vin > VDD + Vtn → NMOS M1 turns on and pulls Vout up to ≈VDD – Vtn.  
 • Vin < –|Vtp|     → PMOS M2 turns on and pulls Vout down to ≈|Vtp| above ground.  
This illustrates that the circuit can work only when the input is driven beyond the supply rails—an unrealistic requirement in ordinary digital logic.

5. Body-diode issue  
Because the sources are tied to the “wrong” rails, the intrinsic body diodes of the two transistors now point from Vout toward both supplies.  
 • If some other circuit forces Vout above VDD by more than a diode drop, M1’s body diode conducts and clamps Vout at VDD + 0.7 V.  
 • If Vout is forced below 0 V by more than a diode drop, M2’s body diode conducts and clamps Vout at –0.7 V.  
Thus the circuit behaves more like a pair of protection diodes than like a logic gate.

6. Static power and noise margins  
• In the legal input range (0 V ≤ Vin ≤ VDD) both devices are OFF, so no static current flows (apart from leakage).  
• The transfer characteristic is a flat “Hi-Z” line; the noise margins are therefore zero—the gate provides no valid logic output levels.

Summary  
Figure 11(b) is not a functioning inverter. With normal 0-to-VDD inputs both transistors remain cut off, leaving the output floating and undefined. The configuration also places the body diodes in a position where they can be forward-biased by out-of-range voltages, turning the pair into nothing more than an over-voltage clamp. This example underlines why, in CMOS logic, the PMOS source must be tied to the upper rail and the NMOS source to the lower rail.

Figure 11(b) is obtained by putting an n-channel device at the top rail and a p-channel device at the bottom rail – exactly the opposite of what is done in a correct CMOS inverter (Fig 11(a)).  
Let  

• M1 = n-MOSFET (connected between VDD and Vout)  
• M2 = p-MOSFET (connected between Vout and GND)  

Operation for the two static input limits:

1. Vin = 0 V (logic “0”)  
   – M1 (n-MOS): VGS = 0 V  ⇒ OFF  
   – M2 (p-MOS): VSG = VS – VG = 0 V – 0 V = 0 V  (< |VTP|) ⇒ OFF  
   → No conducting path to either rail; the output node is left floating (high--Z).  
     Whatever charge was stored on Cout will remain, so the gate does not force a logic level.

2. Vin = VDD (logic “1”)  
   – M1 (n-MOS): VGS = VDD – Vout ≥ VTN  ⇒ ON  
   – M2 (p-MOS): VSG = 0 V – VDD = –VDD (<0, not >|VTP|) ⇒ OFF  
   → Vout is charged through the n-MOS device, but that device is arranged as a
     source follower (common-drain): it conducts only until  
        Vout ≈ VDD – VTN .  
     Thus the highest output level obtainable is VDD minus one n-channel
     threshold; the rail-to-rail logic “1” of a normal CMOS inverter is never
     reached.  
   → No path exists to discharge the output to ground, so a logic “0” can never
     be actively produced.

Transfer characteristic

• For Vin < VTN : both devices OFF ⇒ Vout = “previous value” (floating).  
• For Vin ≥ VTN : Mn enters conduction ⇒ Vout ≈ Vin – VTN  (max ≅ VDD – VTN).  
• Mp is OFF for every possible Vin between 0 V and VDD.

Consequences

1. The stage is not an inverter; it is a non-inverting source-follower that never
   drives a low level and supplies a degraded high level.  
2. Noise margins are essentially zero because the output never reaches either
   supply rail.  
3. Static power dissipation is low (only one device can be ON), but the gate is
   useless for digital logic: it cannot produce valid CMOS-level “0” and “1”.  

In short, Fig 11(b) is a malformed CMOS inverter whose output is either high-impedance or a threshold-dropped version of the input; it cannot serve as a functional logic gate.

Let  

 M1 = the upper n-MOSFET (drain tied to VDD, gate = Vin, source = Vout, body at 0)  
 M2 = the lower p-MOSFET (drain tied to 0, gate = Vin, source = Vout, body tied to VDD).  

(The transistors are therefore in the opposite positions to those in a proper CMOS inverter.)

1. Conditions for the two devices to conduct  

   n-MOS (M1) is ON if VGS1 = Vin – Vout ≥ Vtn     (1)  
   p-MOS (M2) is ON if VSG2 = Vout – Vin ≥ |Vtp(eff)|  (2)

   |Vtp(eff)| is larger than the zero-bias |Vtp0| because the p-device’s
   body is at VDD while its source can fall far below VDD
   (large body-effect term γ√(2φF + |VSB|) ).

2. DC behaviour for the two logic-level inputs

   a) Vin = 0  

      • M1 : VGS1 = –Vout < 0  ⇒ OFF  
      • M2 : VSG2 = Vout – 0 = Vout  
              The largest value Vout can ever reach is VDD, so  
              VSG2 ≤ VDD – 0 ­ < |Vtp(eff)|. ⇒ M2 is also OFF.  

      Result: both transistors are off and Vout is high-impedance.  
      The node keeps whatever charge it had; a fresh circuit that
      starts with Vout = 0 will simply stay near 0 V.  
      A valid, strongly driven logic ‘0’ is therefore never produced.

   b) Vin = VDD  

      • M1 : VGS1 = VDD – Vout.  
              Initially Vout ≈ 0 so VGS1 ≥ Vtn → M1 turns ON and
              charges Vout upward.  Conduction stops when
              VGS1 falls to Vtn, i.e. when Vout ≈ VDD – Vtn.  

      • M2 : VSG2 = Vout – VDD ≈ –Vtn < 0 (< |Vtp(eff)|) → OFF.  

      Result: Vout is pulled only to VDD – Vtn (a “weak-1”, lower
      than a real logic ‘1’).

3. Mid-range inputs and possible simultaneous conduction  

   Because condition (1) requires Vin ≥ Vout + Vtn  
   while condition (2) requires  Vin ≤ Vout – |Vtp(eff)|,  

   the two inequalities can never be satisfied at the same time
   (Vtn + |Vtp(eff)| is positive).  Therefore M1 and M2 are
   never on simultaneously and there is no direct VDD–to-GND
   short-circuit, but there is a wide range of Vin for which
   both devices are off and the output simply floats.

4. Transfer characteristic

   • For Vin < Vtn → M1 off, M2 off  → Vout is indeterminate (Hi-Z).  
   • For Vin ≥ Vtn → M1 behaves as a source follower, giving  
                     Vout = Vin – Vtn  until it tops out at
                     VDD – Vtn.  
   • M2 never pulls the node low because its source is held well
     below its body, raising its threshold far above any possible
     VSG2 value.

5. Consequences

   • The gate never delivers a valid logic ‘0’.  
   • The logic ‘1’ is degraded by one n-MOS threshold.  
   • There are no usable noise margins.  
   • The circuit therefore is not an inverter at all; it is merely a
     poor source-follower that leaves its output floating whenever
     Vin is low.

In short, placing an n-MOS at the top rail and a p-MOS at the
bottom (Figure 11-b) destroys the fundamental pull-up / pull-down
operation of a CMOS inverter and yields a useless, indeterminate
“logic” element.

NMOS cascode gain stage (Figure 15)  
M1 = input device, M2 = cascode device, I1 = bias current source, Vb1 = dc bias that fixes the source of M2 at node X.

A. DC (bias) conditions

1. Current in the branch is fixed by the current source: ID1 ≈ ID2 = I1  
2. To keep both transistors in saturation we must have  

   •  VDS1 = VX ≥ VOV1 (≈ VGS1 – VTH1)  
   •  VDS2 = VOUT – VX ≥ VOV2  

   With a chosen over-drive VOV2 the required value of VX is fixed by
        VX = Vb1 – (VTH2 + VOV2) .
   The bias voltage Vb1 therefore sets VX and at the same time guarantees that M2 stays in saturation as long as the output node is not pulled too far down.

B. Small-signal model

gm1 , ro1 : transconductance and small-signal drain-source resistance of M1  
gm2 , ro2 : corresponding quantities of M2  
roI : incremental resistance of the current source (→ ∞ for an ideal source)

C. Output resistance (set vin = 0 and apply a test current Io at Vout)

   Rout = roI || ( ro2 + (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1 )

   For an ideal current source roI → ∞, so

   Rout ≈ ro2 + (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1
         ≈ gm2 ro2 ro1   if gm2 ro2 » 1.

   Hence the cascode roughly multiplies the bottom-device resistance ro1 by the gain gm2 ro2 of the cascode device.

D. Voltage gain

Because the MOS gate has an (almost) infinite resistance Rin ≈ ∞, the small-signal input current is zero and the input node sees only the gate capacitance.

With the output resistance found above:

   Av = vout / vin =  – gm1 · ( Rout )

   =  – gm1 · ( roI || [ ro2 + (1 + gm2 ro2) ro1 ] )

   For an ideal current source and gm2 ro2 » 1,

   Av ≈  – gm1 gm2 ro1 ro2

   In terms of intrinsic gain (gm / gds = gm ro) of each transistor:

        |Av| ≈ ( gm1 ro1 ) · ( gm2 ro2 )

   Thus the magnitude of the gain is the product of the intrinsic gains of the two stacked devices (often several thousand in modern processes).

E. Node-X gain (how well the cascode suppresses the swinging of the drain of M1)

   vX / vin = – gm1 ro1 / ( 1 + gm2 ro2 + ro1/ro2 )

   ≈ – ( gm1 ro1 ) / ( gm2 ro2 ) if gm2 ro2 » 1.

   With gm2 ro2 in the tens to hundreds, node X moves only a few per-cent of the output swing, reducing the Miller capacitance that would otherwise limit bandwidth.

F. Summary of the stage characteristics

• Very high small-signal voltage gain because Rout is boosted by the cascode.  
• Very high output resistance, approaching gm2 ro2 ro1.  
• Nearly infinite input resistance (capacitive input).  
• Small signal swing at the sensitive drain of the input device, improving speed.  
• Proper choice of Vb1 is essential to keep both MOSFETs in saturation over the required output swing.

These properties make the simple NMOS cascode a standard high-gain building block in CMOS analog design.

The two n-channel transistors are stacked so that

• M1 is the input (common-source) device, whose drain is tied to the source of  
• M2, whose gate is held at the fixed bias voltage Vb1 so that M2 operates as a common-gate device.

Because the gate of M2 is fixed, any change that tries to appear at the drain of M1 is “absorbed” by the large intrinsic gain of the common-gate stage, keeping the drain of M1 almost at a constant voltage.  
This local feedback

– keeps M1 in saturation,  
– greatly increases the small-signal output resistance seen at the drain of M2, and  
– therefore raises the overall voltage gain.

Those are exactly the properties for which a cascode is used.  
The resistor RD is only the load that converts the current of the cascode branch into a voltage; replacing it with an active current source would raise the gain further, but the presence of a resistor does not change the fact that M1–M2 form a cascode pair.

Yes.  
A MOS-cascode is obtained when

1. The signal-carrying device (here M1) is used in common-source so its drain current contains the input information, and  
2. A second device (here M2) is stacked on top of it with its gate held at a fixed dc bias Vb1 so that it operates in common-gate.

With M2 in common-gate, small-signal variations that appear at its drain (the output node) are strongly attenuated before they reach its source, so the drain-to-source voltage of M1 remains almost constant. This raises the overall output resistance to roughly

Rout ≈ ro1 · gm2 · ro2

—the hallmark of a cascode.  
The resistor RD is merely the load that converts the stack current into an output voltage; it does not change the fact that the pair M1–M2 constitutes a cascode. The only requirement is that Vb1 be chosen so that both transistors stay in saturation over the intended signal swing.

Yes.

The two MOSFETs form the classic CS–CG stack that defines a cascode pair:

• M1 is a common-source (CS) device – its source is at ac ground, its gate is the signal input, and the signal current flows through its drain.

• M2 sits directly on top of M1 with its gate fixed at the bias voltage Vb1. For small-signal purposes that makes M2 a common-gate (CG) device, so the current coming from M1 is “handed off’’ to M2 and leaves at M2’s drain.

The cascade of a CS stage driving a CG stage in the same current path is what the word cascode means, independent of what is used as the load. In this schematic the load happens to be a resistor RD rather than the more usual current-source transistor, but that only lowers the output resistance and gain—it does not change the topology.

Therefore the circuit of Figure 16 is indeed a cascode structure (a resistor-loaded MOS cascode amplifier).

Based on the circuit diagram in Figure 11(a), here is the analysis:

### 1. Circuit Identification
The circuit shown in Figure 11(a) is a **CMOS Inverter** (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Inverter). It is the fundamental building block of CMOS digital logic circuits.

### 2. Component Analysis
The circuit consists of two MOSFETs connected in series between the supply voltage $V_{DD}$ and ground:
*   **$M_2$ (Top Transistor):** This is a **PMOS** transistor.
    *   Its **Source** is connected to $V_{DD}$.
    *   Its **Gate** is connected to the input $V_{\text{in}}$.
    *   Its **Drain** is connected to the output $V_{\text{out}}$.
    *   It acts as the **pull-up network**. The arrow on the symbol points inward/towards the gate, which is a common representation for PMOS (indicating the p-type channel).
*   **$M_1$ (Bottom Transistor):** This is an **NMOS** transistor.
    *   Its **Source** is connected to Ground (GND).
    *   Its **Gate** is connected to the input $V_{\text{in}}$.
    *   Its **Drain** is connected to the output $V_{\text{out}}$.
    *   It acts as the **pull-down network**. The arrow points outward, typical for NMOS representation.

### 3. Operation Analysis (Logic Levels)
The circuit functions as a logical **NOT** gate (inverter). The output state depends on the input voltage $V_{\text{in}}$ relative to the threshold voltages of the transistors ($V_{TN}$ for NMOS and $|V_{TP}|$ for PMOS).

*   **Case 1: Input is Low ($V_{\text{in}} \approx 0$ V)**
    *   **$M_1$ (NMOS):** $V_{GS} = 0 < V_{TN}$. The transistor is **OFF** (cutoff). No current flows to ground.
    *   **$M_2$ (PMOS):** $V_{SG} = V_{DD} - 0 = V_{DD} > |V_{TP}|$. The transistor is **ON** (conducting).
    *   **Result:** The output $V_{\text{out}}$ is connected to $V_{DD}$ through the conducting $M_2$. Thus, **$V_{\text{out}} = V_{DD}$ (Logic High)**.

*   **Case 2: Input is High ($V_{\text{in}} \approx V_{DD}$)**
    *   **$M_1$ (NMOS):** $V_{GS} = V_{DD} > V_{TN}$. The transistor is **ON** (conducting).
    *   **$M_2$ (PMOS):** $V_{SG} = V_{DD} - V_{DD} = 0 < |V_{TP}|$. The transistor is **OFF** (cutoff). No current flows from $V_{DD}$.
    *   **Result:** The output $V_{\text{out}}$ is connected to Ground through the conducting $M_1$. Thus, **$V_{\text{out}} = 0$ V (Logic Low)**.

*   **Case 3: Transition Region ($V_{TN} < V_{\text{in}} < V_{DD} - |V_{TP}|$)**
    *   Both transistors can be in the saturation or linear (triode) region.
    *   As $V_{\text{in}}$ increases, $V_{\text{out}}$ decreases sharply. This region provides high voltage gain and is used for analog amplification, but in digital logic, it represents the switching transition.

### 4. Key Characteristics
*   **Inversion:** The output is the logical inverse of the input ($V_{\text{out}} = \overline{V_{\text{in}}}$).
*   **Static Power Dissipation:** Ideally, there is **zero static power consumption**. In steady state (Logic 0 or Logic 1), one transistor is always OFF, creating an open circuit between $V_{DD}$ and Ground. No direct current path exists. (Power is only consumed during the switching transient or due to leakage currents).
*   **Noise Margin:** CMOS inverters have excellent noise margins because the output swings fully from rail to rail ($0$ to $V_{DD}$).
*   **High Input Impedance:** Since the gates of MOSFETs are insulated (oxide layer), the input draws negligible DC current.

**Summary:** Figure 11(a) depicts a standard CMOS inverter where $M_2$ (PMOS) pulls the output high when the input is low, and $M_1$ (NMOS) pulls the output low when the input is high.

Based on the circuit diagram in Figure 11(a), here is the analysis:

### 1. Circuit Identification
The circuit shown in Figure 11(a) is a **CMOS Inverter** (Complementary Metal-Oxide-Semiconductor Inverter). It is the fundamental building block of CMOS logic circuits.

### 2. Component Analysis
The circuit consists of two transistors connected in a specific series configuration:
*   **$M_2$ (Top Transistor):** This is a **PMOS** transistor.
    *   **Source:** Connected to $V_{DD}$ (supply voltage).
    *   **Gate:** Connected to the input $V_{in}$.
    *   **Drain:** Connected to the output $V_{out}$.
    *   **Function:** It acts as the **pull-up device**. It turns on when the input voltage is low ($V_{in} < V_{DD} - |V_{THP}|$), connecting the output to $V_{DD}$. The arrow pointing towards the gate (or indicating the p-n junction direction) is characteristic of a PMOS symbol in this context.

*   **$M_1$ (Bottom Transistor):** This is an **NMOS** transistor.
    *   **Source:** Connected to Ground (GND).
    *   **Gate:** Connected to the input $V_{in}$.
    *   **Drain:** Connected to the output $V_{out}$.
    *   **Function:** It acts as the **pull-down device**. It turns on when the input voltage is high ($V_{in} > V_{THN}$), connecting the output to Ground.

### 3. Circuit Operation (Voltage Transfer Characteristic)
The circuit operates as a logic gate that inverts the input signal. Let's analyze the output voltage $V_{out}$ for different input states:

*   **Case 1: Input Low ($V_{in} = 0$ V or Logic '0')**
    *   **NMOS ($M_1$):** $V_{GS1} = V_{in} - 0 = 0$ V. Since $0 < V_{THN}$ (threshold voltage), $M_1$ is in **cutoff (OFF)**. No current flows from drain to source.
    *   **PMOS ($M_2$):** $V_{SG2} = V_{DD} - V_{in} = V_{DD}$. Since $V_{DD} > |V_{THP}|$, $M_2$ is **ON** (conducting). It acts like a closed switch connecting $V_{out}$ to $V_{DD}$.
    *   **Result:** $V_{out} \approx V_{DD}$ (Logic '1').

*   **Case 2: Input High ($V_{in} = V_{DD}$ or Logic '1')**
    *   **NMOS ($M_1$):** $V_{GS1} = V_{in} - 0 = V_{DD}$. Since $V_{DD} > V_{THN}$, $M_1$ is **ON** (conducting). It acts like a closed switch connecting $V_{out}$ to Ground.
    *   **PMOS ($M_2$):** $V_{SG2} = V_{DD} - V_{in} = 0$ V. Since $0 < |V_{THP}|$, $M_2$ is in **cutoff (OFF)**. No current flows from $V_{DD}$ to $V_{out}$.
    *   **Result:** $V_{out} \approx 0$ V (Logic '0').

*   **Case 3: Transition Region ($0 < V_{in} < V_{DD}$)**

### 1. Circuit Identification

*   **$M_1$**: The input transistor operating in a **Common Source (CS)** configuration. Its gate receives the input signal $V_{in}$, its source is grounded, and its drain is connected to the source of $M_2$ (node X).
*   **$M_2$**: The cascode transistor operating in a **Common Gate (CG)** configuration. Its gate is biased by a DC voltage $V_{b1}$ (which is an AC ground), its source is connected to node X, and its drain is the output node $V_{out}$.
*   **$I_1$**: An active load (current source) connected to $V_{DD}$. It sets the bias current for the stage and provides the output resistance for the amplifier.

### 2. DC Analysis (Biasing)
*   The current source $I_1$ establishes a DC bias current $I_D \approx I_1$ flowing through $M_2$ and $M_1$.
*   $V_{b1}$ is chosen to keep $M_2$ in saturation. Specifically, $V_{GS2} = V_{b1} - V_X$. For $M_2$ to be in saturation, we need $V_{DS2} \ge V_{GS2} - V_{th}$, or $V_{out} - V_X \ge V_{b1} - V_{th} - V_{th}$.
*   $M_1$ is kept in saturation by ensuring $V_X \ge V_{in} - V_{th}$ (overdrive voltage condition).

### 3. Small-Signal Analysis
To analyze the gain and impedance, we use the small-signal model. Let's define the parameters:
*   $g_{m1}, r_{o1}$: Transconductance and output resistance of $M_1$.
*   $g_{m2}, r_{o2}$: Transconductance and output resistance of $M_2$. (Note: Since the source of $M_2$ is at node X (not ground), there is a body effect, so we can use an effective transconductance $g_{m2}' = g_{m2} + g_{mb2}$).
*   $R_{SS}$ (or $r_{o, load}$): The output resistance of the current source $I_1$. In an ideal analysis, this is $\infty$, but in practice, it is finite (determined by the transistor generating $I_1$).

#### A. Input Impedance ($R_{in}$)
The input is applied to the gate of $M_1$. Since the gate of a MOSFET draws no DC current and has infinite impedance at low frequencies:
$$R_{in} = \infty$$

#### B. Output Impedance ($R_{out}$)
The output resistance is determined by looking into the output node $V_{out}$.
1.  **Looking down (into the cascode stack $M_2-M_1$):** The cascode configuration significantly boosts the output resistance. The resistance looking into the drain of $M_2$ is approximately:
    $$R_{down} \approx (g_{m2} + g_{mb2}) r_{o2} r_{o1}$$
    *(More precisely: $R_{down} = r_{o2} + r_{o1} + (g_{m2} + g_{mb2})r_{o2}r_{o1} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$ for large $g_m r_o$)*.
2.  **Looking up (into the load $I_1$):** The current source has a finite output resistance, let's call it $R_{SS}$ (or $r_{o3}$ if implemented by a transistor).
3.  **Total Output Resistance:**
    $$R_{out} = R_{down} \parallel R_{SS} \approx \left[ (g_{m2} + g_{mb2}) r_{o2} r_{o1} \right] \parallel R_{SS}$$

#### C. Voltage Gain ($A_v$)
The voltage gain is given by $A_v = -G_m R_{out}$, where $G_m$ is the equivalent transconductance of the stage.

1.  **Effective Transconductance ($G_m$):**
    The input voltage $v_{in}$ creates a current $g_{m1}v_{in}$ in $M_1$. Because the input impedance looking into the source of $M_2$ is low ($\approx 1/g_{m2}'$), almost all of this current is passed through to the output.
    $$G_m \approx g_{m1}$$
    *(Technically, there is a slight current division between $r_{o1}$ and the input resistance of $M_2$, but for high gain stages, $G_m \approx g_{m1}$)*.

2.  **Gain Calculation:**
    The output voltage is the output current times the total output resistance. Since an increase in $v_{in}$ increases the downward current, $v_{out}$ decreases (inverted).
    $$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} \approx -g_{m1} \cdot R_{out}$$
    $$A_v \approx -g_{m1} \left[ \left( (g_{m2} + g_{mb2}) r_{o2} r_{o1} \right) \parallel R_{SS} \right]$$

    **Special Case (Ideal Current Source Load):**
    If we assume the current source $I_1$ is ideal ($R_{SS} \to \infty$), the gain becomes:
    $$A_v \approx -g_{m1} (g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1})$$
    This is approximately $-(g_{m1}r_{o1})(g_{m2}r_{o2})$, which is proportional to the square of the intrinsic gain ($g_m r_o$). This is much higher than a simple Common Source amplifier with a resistive load (gain $\approx g_m r_o$).

### 4. Key Characteristics & Benefits
*   **High Gain:** As derived above, the gain is roughly $(g_m r_o)^2$, which is very high for a single stage.
*   **High Output Impedance:** The cascode structure makes the output impedance very high (proportional to $g_m r_o^2$), which is excellent for voltage amplification when loaded by another high-impedance node or a current source.
*   **Bandwidth (Miller Effect Reduction):** In a simple high-gain Common Source amplifier, the gate-drain capacitance $C_{gd}$ is multiplied by the gain (Miller effect), reducing bandwidth. In this cascode stage:
    *   The gain of the first stage ($M_1$) is low. The load at the drain of $M_1$ (node X) is the input resistance of $M_2$, which is $\approx 1/g_{m2}$.
    *   Voltage gain of $M_1$ stage: $A_{v1} \approx -g_{m1} (1/g_{m2}) \approx -1$.
    *   Because the gain of the first stage is close to -1, the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is minimal ($C_{in} \approx C_{gs1} + 2C_{gd1}$). This results in a **much wider bandwidth** compared to a simple high-gain CS stage.

### Summary Equation
The voltage gain of the circuit is approximately:
$$ A_v \approx -g_{m1} \left( R_{out, cascode} \parallel R_{load} \right) $$
Where $R_{out, cascode} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$ and $R_{load}$ is the output resistance of the current source $I_1$.

The total output resistance at node $V_{out}$ is the parallel combination of the resistance looking down into the cascode stack ($M_2, M_1$) and the resistance looking up into the current source load.

1.  **Resistance looking down ($R_{down}$)**:
    Looking into the drain of $M_2$, we see the output resistance of a cascode structure. The source of $M_2$ is connected to the drain of $M_1$, which has a resistance of $r_{o1}$ to ground.
    $$R_{down} = r_{o2} + (1 + g_{m2}r_{o2})r_{o1} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$$
    (This is a very high resistance, typically much larger than $r_{o1}$ or $r_{o2}$ alone).

2.  **Resistance looking up ($R_{up}$)**:
    Looking into the current source $I_1$, we see its output resistance, let's call it $r_{o,load}$. (If the current source is ideal, this is $\infty$).

3.  **Total Output Resistance**:
    $$R_{out, total} = R_{down} \parallel R_{up} = (g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}) \parallel r_{o,load}$$

**B. Voltage Gain ($A_v$)**
The circuit acts as a transconductance amplifier.
1.  **Effective Transconductance ($G_m$)**:
    The input voltage $v_{in}$ creates a current $g_{m1}v_{in}$ in $M_1$. This current is passed through $M_2$ to the output node. The cascode structure has a current gain of approximately 1 (for high $r_o$).
    $$i_{out} \approx g_{m1}v_{in}$$
    So, $G_m \approx g_{m1}$.

2.  **Gain Calculation**:
    The output voltage is the product of the output current and the total load resistance. Since the current $g_{m1}v_{in}$ flows from $V_{out}$ to ground (pulling current down), the gain is negative.
    $$A_v = \frac{v_{out}}{v_{in}} = -G_m \cdot R_{out, total}$$
    $$A_v \approx -g_{m1} \left[ (g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}) \parallel r_{o,load} \right]$$

    *   **Case 1: Ideal Current Source ($r_{o,load} \to \infty$)**
        $$A_v \approx -g_{m1} (g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1})$$
        This results in a very high voltage gain, proportional to the product of transconductances and output resistances ($g^2 r^4$ dependence roughly).

    *   **Case 2: Non-ideal Current Source (Finite $r_{o,load}$)**
        Since $g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1} \gg r_{o,load}$ usually, the total resistance is dominated by the current source's resistance.
        $$A_v \approx -g_{m1} r_{o,load}$$
        In this case, the gain is similar to a simple Common-Source amplifier with a current source load.

### 4. Key Advantages of this Topology
Although the DC gain might be limited by the load resistance (in Case 2), this cascode configuration offers significant advantages over a simple Common-Source stage:

1.  **Increased Bandwidth (Reduced Miller Effect)**:
    *   In a simple CS amplifier, the drain capacitance $C_{gd}$ is multiplied by the gain $(1 + |A_v|)$ due to the Miller effect, creating a large input capacitance that limits bandwidth.
    *   In this cascode circuit, the voltage gain from the input ($V_{in}$) to node X ($V_X$) is very small. $V_X \approx -v_{in} \frac{r_{o1} \parallel (1/g_{m2})}{1} \approx -v_{in} \frac{g_{m1}}{g_{m2}}$. If transistors are matched, the gain to node X is $\approx -1$.
    *   Because the gain of the first stage ($M_1$) is low, the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ is minimal. The input capacitance is roughly $C_{gs1} + 2C_{gd1}$, which is much smaller than in a simple CS stage. This significantly **increases the bandwidth** (high $f_T$).

2.  **High Output Impedance**:
    *   The resistance looking down into the drain of $M_2$ is $g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$, which is very high. If the load $I_1$ were a resistor $R_D$ instead of a current source, the gain would be $-g_{m1}(R_{down} \parallel R_D) \approx -g_{m1}R_D$. This allows for high gain using a resistor without the Miller effect penalty. (Here, the load is a current source, so the high output impedance is useful for driving capacitive loads or as part of a larger differential pair with active load).

3.  **Improved Output Swing**:
    *   The cascode structure allows the output voltage $V_{out}$ to swing lower while keeping the input transistor $M_1$ in saturation. In a simple CS with a current source load, the minimum output voltage is limited by the load transistor's saturation voltage. Here, $V_{out,min} \approx V_{b1} - V_{th}$. By choosing $V_{b1}$ appropriately, the linear output range can be optimized.

### Summary
*   **Circuit**: NMOS Cascode Amplifier.
*   **Gain**: $A_v \approx -g_{m1} ( (g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}) \parallel r_{o,load} )$.
*   **Main Benefit**: High bandwidth due to the elimination of the Miller effect at the input stage, and high output impedance looking down from $V_{out}$.

### 1. Circuit Identification
The circuit shown is an **NMOS Cascode Amplifier** with an ideal current source load.
*   **$M_1$**: This is the input transistor configured as a **Common-Source (CS)** amplifier. It converts the input voltage $V_{in}$ into a current.
*   **$M_2$**: This is the cascode transistor configured as a **Common-Gate (CG)** amplifier. It acts as a current buffer, passing the current from $M_1$ to the output while providing high output impedance.
*   **$I_1$**: This is an ideal current source connected to $V_{DD}$. It serves two purposes:
    *   It sets the DC bias current for the stack ($I_{D1} = I_{D2} = I_1$).
    *   It acts as the load for the amplifier. Since it is an ideal current source, it has infinite small-signal impedance.
*   **$V_{b1}$**: This is a constant DC bias voltage applied to the gate of $M_2$ to keep it in the saturation region.

### 2. Small-Signal Analysis

To find the voltage gain ($A_v$), we need to determine the effective transconductance ($G_m$) and the total output resistance ($R_{out}$).

**A. Effective Transconductance ($G_m$)**
The input voltage $v_{in}$ is applied to the gate of $M_1$. This generates a small-signal drain current:
$$i_{d1} = g_{m1} v_{in}$$
The cascode transistor $M_2$ (common-gate stage) has a low input impedance at its source (node X, approximately $1/g_{m2}$) and passes this current to the drain with a current gain of approximately unity. Therefore, the effective transconductance of the entire stage is dominated by $M_1$:
$$G_m \approx g_{m1}$$

**B. Output Resistance ($R_{out}$)**
The output resistance at node $V_{out}$ is the parallel combination of the impedance looking up into the current source and the impedance looking down into the cascode stack.
*   **Looking up:** The ideal current source $I_1$ has infinite impedance ($R_{load} = \infty$).
*   **Looking down:** The impedance looking into the drain of the cascode transistor $M_2$ is significantly boosted. The resistance at the source of $M_2$ (node X) is the output resistance of $M_1$, which is $r_{o1}$. The cascode configuration boosts this resistance by a factor of roughly $(g_{m2} r_{o2})$.
    $$R_{down} \approx r_{o2} + r_{o1} + g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1} \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$$
    (Assuming $g_{m2}r_{o2} \gg 1$)

So, the total output resistance is:
$$R_{out} = R_{load} \parallel R_{down} = \infty \parallel (g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}) \approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$$

**C. Voltage Gain ($A_v$)**
The small-signal voltage gain is given by $A_v = -G_m R_{out}$.
$$A_v \approx -g_{m1} (g_{m2} r_{o2} r_{o1})$$

If we assume the transistors are identical ($g_{m1} \approx g_{m2} = g_m$ and $r_{o1} \approx r_{o2} = r_o$), the gain becomes:
$$A_v \approx -(g_m r_o)^2$$
This represents a very high voltage gain, essentially the square of the intrinsic gain of a single transistor.

### 3. Key Characteristics and Advantages

1.  **High Gain:** As derived above, the use of a cascode structure with a high-impedance current source load results in a very large voltage gain, proportional to $(g_m r_o)^2$.
2.  **High Output Impedance:** The output impedance is very high ($\approx g_{m2}r_{o2}r_{o1}$), which is desirable for high-gain amplifier stages.
3.  **Reduced Miller Effect:** In a simple common-source amplifier, the gate-drain capacitance ($C_{gd}$) of the transistor is multiplied by the gain (Miller effect), limiting bandwidth. In this cascode circuit, the drain of $M_1$ (node X) is a low-impedance node (approximately $1/g_{m2}$). This "shields" the input $V_{in}$ from the large voltage swings at $V_{out}$, significantly reducing the Miller multiplication of $C_{gd1}$ and improving the high-frequency response (bandwidth).
4.  **Biasing:** For proper operation, $V_{b1}$ must be chosen such that both $M_1$ and $M_2$ remain in saturation. Typically, $V_{b1} \approx V_{GS2} + V_{DS1,sat}$ (or $V_{TH2} + 2V_{ov}$ if overdrive voltages are equal), ensuring $M_1$ is at the edge of saturation and $M_2$ is on.
